S12-01.note: B (1/12) is the subtract-instead-of-multiply path, A (3/8) is halving; both are real student errors.

S12-02.solved: 7 parts = 84, one part = 12, Noah has 4 parts = 48.
S12-02.note: Stem names Mia as the smaller share, which removes the usual who-gets-which ambiguity. D (36) is Mia's share.

S12-03.note: D (2) is the GCF and no student route produces it as a 'least common multiple'; C (1728) is the raw product. One clearly dead option in a five-wide set.

S12-04.note: E (210) stops after the first step, C (330) applies both to 300, B (189) subtracts 10% instead of adding. All four wrong paths are named.

S12-05.solved: Middle term = 310/5 = 62; the five are 58,60,62,64,66, so the largest is 66.
S12-05.note: A (58) smallest, B (62) middle, E (64) off-by-one-step. C (72) is loose.

S12-06.note: Arithmetic is fine by hand. A (2.67) is 8/3 (dropping the .2), C (0.4) is the reciprocal, D (25.6) multiplies.

S12-07.note: WORDING: 'x squared plus 1 divided by x squared' is ambiguous in plain text - it can be read as (x^2 + 1)/x^2. That reading gives 1 + 1/x^2, which is not among the options, so no second letter becomes defensible, but the stem should be rendered as x^2 + 1/x^2 (or with explicit parentheses) before it ships. E (25) is the forgot-the-2 trap and is the strongest distractor in the batch. This is the hardest item here and sits at the top of the SSAT Upper range.

S12-08.note: A (15) forgets to divide, E (15/7) adds the x-terms, D (3) is a sign slip.

S12-09.note: D (4.75) and E (3.5) come from mis-parsing which side gets the +5; B (12) from 3n = n + 19 - ... loose but reachable.

S12-10.note: The option set is the full cross of sign error x flip error (x > -3, x < 3, x > 3). Textbook-clean.

S12-11.solved: Add the equations: 5x + 5y = 30, so x + y = 6.
S12-11.note: C (15) and E (30) are the un-divided sums; A (4) is x - y.

S12-12.second_defensible: A (83), if 'raised to the power x + 2' is read as 3^x + 2 = 81 + 2 = 83. The render has no parentheses and no superscript, so the exponent's extent is genuinely undetermined in the text a student sees - and unlike S12-07 the alternate reading lands exactly on a listed option, which is what makes it live rather than academic.
S12-12.note: Fix the stem to read '3^(x+2)' or 'three raised to the power (x + 2)'. As rendered, A is not a distractor, it is a second key under a defensible parse. This is the one item in the batch I would hold.

S12-13.solved: Area ratio 9:25 -> side ratio 3:5 -> perimeter ratio 3:5; 36 x 5/3 = 60.
S12-13.note: C (100) applies the area ratio to the perimeter; E (21.6) inverts the ratio. The similar-figures scaling rule is the single idea being tested.

S12-14.note: E (48) is 3w^2 with w from the full perimeter; A (96) halves the area.

S12-15.note: B (54) and E (84) are the other two angles - the classic answer-the-wrong-part trap, and both are live here.

S12-16.note: D (25) stops at s^2, B (30) is 150/5, C (3375) cubes 15.

S12-17.solved: Base along the x-axis from (0,0) to (6,0) is 6; height is the y-coordinate 5; area = 6*5/2 = 15.
S12-17.note: E (30) forgets the half. The x = 2 of the apex is a deliberate red herring (D = 6 uses 2 and 6 as legs); good. No figure needed, and none is supplied - correct.

S12-18.solved: Square 10x10 = 100; quarter circle = (1/4)*pi*10^2 = 25pi; remaining = 100 - 25pi, so k = 25.
S12-18.note: A (100) uses the full circle, B (50) halves it, E (10) is the radius. A quarter circle of radius 10 centred on a corner of a 10-cm square fits exactly, so the described region is unambiguous without a figure.

S12-19.solved: Start: height = sqrt(625 - 49) = sqrt(576) = 24. After: foot at 15, height = sqrt(625 - 225) = sqrt(400) = 20. Slide = 24 - 20 = 4.
S12-19.note: Two Pythagorean triples chained (7-24-25, 15-20-25) so it is exact by hand. E (8) is the horizontal pull mistaken for the vertical drop - the trap the item is built around, and a strong one. Second-hardest item in the batch.

S12-20.note: D (18000) skips the unit conversion, A (30) uses the tank's full 30 cm depth as if it were the answer. The 30 cm depth is an unused given, which is fair.

S12-21.note: A (90) is the new total, E (15) the new mean, D (19) a near-miss. Pairs with S12-24 - same total-then-difference idea run forwards and backwards. Not a duplicate, but a form should probably not carry both.

S12-22.solved: After one green is removed and kept out: 5 green remain of 14 marbles; probability 5/14.
S12-22.note: E (6/14) forgets to decrement the numerator, C (5/13) decrements the total twice, B (6/15) ignores the first draw entirely. 'kept out of the bag' makes the without-replacement condition explicit - good, since that is the usual source of dispute on this item type.

S12-23.solved: C(7,3) = 35 total committees; all-girl committees C(4,3) = 4; 35 - 4 = 31.
S12-23.note: C (35) is the un-subtracted total, D (34) subtracts 1 instead of 4, B (18) is an ordered/partial count. Combinations with a complement step is at the top edge of SSAT Upper Level - legitimate but this is the third genuinely hard item.

S12-24.note: E (52) is the remaining total, B (12) assumes the mean is unchanged, A (8.67) divides 52 by 6. See the S12-21 note on overlap.
